name: Beaux-Arts (French)

revival_periods.note: Not a revival so much as a transplant: Richard Morris Hunt entered the Ecole in 1846 and roughly 500 Americans followed before 1914, taking the method home wholesale.
The contemporary classical movement re-adopts Beaux-Arts composition and the poche-and-parti method explicitly, and several schools now teach the analytique again.

geography.hearth: The Ecole des Beaux-Arts, rue Bonaparte, Paris

lineage.note: Institutionally continuous: the Ecole is the reorganised successor to the Academie royale's teaching, the Prix de Rome runs unbroken, and Durand's and Blondel's compositional method is what the atelier system transmits.

The Grand Manner is deliberately reclaimed after 1850 - coupled columns, sculptural relief, the pavilion silhouette and the mansard all come back from Louis XIV, not from the Neoclassical generation that had suppressed them.
The scenographic plan, the ceremonial stair and the axial urban set-piece are quoted from Rome; Garnier's grand escalier is a Baroque theatre stage where the audience is the performance.
The palazzo elevation - graded rustication, superimposed orders, heavy crowning cornice - remains the default clothing for commercial and institutional blocks.

description.short: Composition taught as a transmissible method - parti, marche and poche - producing large, richly sculptural, axially planned public buildings whose elevations are direct projections of their plans.
description.long:
The Beaux-Arts is less a set of forms than a way of getting from a programme to a building, and it is the only such method the classical tradition ever fully institutionalised. A student in the atelier system received a programme, was locked in a cubicle for twelve hours to produce an esquisse - the parti, the fundamental diagram - and then spent weeks developing it without being allowed to change the diagram. The plan came first, always, laid out on a dominant axis with cross-axes, with major and minor spaces ranked by size and ceiling height, and with circulation - the marche, the sequence of movement - designed as an experience rather than as leftover corridor. The wall was drawn as poche, a thickened black mass carved out for stairs, closets, flues and lightwells, which is why Beaux-Arts buildings absorb their servicing invisibly. The elevation was then a projection of that hierarchy, and only at the end was the order chosen, according to caractere - the doctrine that a bank, an opera house and a hospital should each look like what they are.

The conditions are industrial and metropolitan. Nineteenth-century Paris needed building types that had never existed at that scale: railway termini, department stores, opera houses, exhibition halls, ministries, apartment blocks of six to eight storeys. It also acquired, under Haussmann from 1853, a state powerful enough to cut boulevards through a medieval city and impose a uniform cornice line on both sides. Behind the stone, everything had changed: rolled iron, then steel, then reinforced concrete, plus lifts, central heating and electric light. The Beaux-Arts settlement was to accept the new structure completely and to let the masonry envelope do a different job - to give a building scale, hierarchy, entrance and civic address. The Grand Palais of 1897-1900 is entirely explicit about this: a Classical stone shell wrapped around a 240-metre iron-and-glass barrel vault, with no attempt at reconciliation and no dishonesty either.

What it reacted against, quietly, was the thinness of its own Neoclassical parent. By 1850 the austere balustraded cube looked bloodless and, worse, insufficiently expressive for a Second Empire that wanted visible magnificence. So sculpture came back onto the wall - not scattered, but concentrated at the entrance, the centre and the skyline - and the mansard came back as an occupiable attic that also restored a silhouette. The result is often criticised as pastiche, and sometimes it is; but the compositional discipline underneath is real and independent of the dress, which is why the same method produced buildings as different as Garnier's Opera and Labrouste's iron-vaulted Bibliotheque Sainte-Genevieve.

What it feels like is arrival, staged. You come at the Palais Garnier along an axis cut for the purpose; the building presents a base you climb, an arcaded loggia, a giant order, and a skyline of gilt figures against the sky. Inside, the auditorium is smaller than you expect, because two-thirds of the building is circulation: a stair hall thirty metres high in coloured marbles with balconies at every level, arranged so that everyone ascending is on display to everyone already up. The plan does exactly what it was drawn to do. This is architecture designed around the truth that in a public building, the most important room is usually the one you pass through.

defining_characteristics: A plan generated first, on a dominant axis with cross-axes, with spaces ranked by size, height and position in the sequence
Poche: the wall drawn and built as a thickened inhabited mass absorbing stairs, services, closets and lightwells
The elevation as a direct projection of the plan's hierarchy - every important room reads on the outside
Three-part vertical composition: rusticated base, principal shaft of one or two storeys under a giant or coupled order, and a crowning attic or mansard
Sculpture concentrated at entrance, centrepiece and skyline rather than distributed over the wall
Caractere: the order and the degree of enrichment chosen to express the building's function and civic standing
Modern structure (iron, steel, reinforced concrete) accepted internally and clothed in a masonry envelope that supplies scale and address
diagnostic_tells: Coupled columns, usually of a giant order, marking a projecting central pavilion on a symmetrical front
A skyline populated with sculpture, quadrigae, cartouches and gilt attic figures above the main cornice
Deeply rusticated ground storey with heavy vermiculated or channelled blocks and segmental-arched openings
A grand exterior or interior stair treated as the principal architectural event, larger than any single room it serves
Enormous scale of the individual member - a keystone the size of a person, garlands two metres across - calibrated to the width of a boulevard rather than a street

distinguished_from.difference: Neoclassicism is subtractive, plane-dominant and unaccented, with the roof hidden and ornament rationed. Beaux-Arts is additive, sculptural and strongly centred, with a visible mansard or attic and enrichment concentrated at the accents.

The American branch works largely in limestone and terracotta on steel frames at greater height, favours the Roman Ionic and Corinthian over French Composite, and typically omits the mansard on commercial buildings. Its plans are Ecole plans; its budgets and its storey counts are not.

Second Empire as usually named is a silhouette style - mansard roof plus pavilions - applied to houses and small civic buildings. Beaux-Arts is a compositional method applied to large programmes; a house with a mansard is Second Empire, an opera house planned about a stair is Beaux-Arts.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Composition by method: parti (the plan diagram), marche (the designed sequence of movement), poche (the thickened, inhabited wall), and caractere (expressive appropriateness of the order). Proportion is hierarchical rather than modular - a room's ceiling height, its position on the axis and its degree of enrichment all encode its rank in the programme.
typical_ratios: Three-part vertical division base : shaft : attic approximately 1 : 2 : 0.5
Rusticated base one to two storeys, 0.25 to 0.35 of total wall height, with joints 25 to 50 mm
Giant order spanning two storeys; coupled columns set 0.5 to 1.0 diameters apart, pairs at 4 to 5 diameters on centre
Entablature 1/4 to 1/5 of column height; crowning cornice projection 1/14 to 1/18 of total facade height
Attic or mansard storey 0.5 to 0.7 of the principal storey height
Principal rooms in the plan set at whole-number multiples of the structural bay, with ceiling heights ranked 1 : 0.75 : 0.6 from major to minor
Grand stair: riser 140-155 mm, tread 340-400 mm, landing every 9 to 11 risers, clear width 1/3 to 1/2 the width of the hall containing it
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Strongly hierarchical and closed at both ends: a dominant centre pavilion, subordinate end pavilions, and a plain connecting rhythm between - commonly 3-2-5-2-3 across a fifteen-bay front. Corners are always resolved with a pavilion, a quoined pier or a change of plane; a Beaux-Arts elevation never simply stops.

massing_affinities.note: The Haussmannian immeuble: six to eight storeys, a uniform cornice line imposed across the whole boulevard, and the block rather than the building as the compositional subject.
The mansard returns as a fully occupiable attic and as the device that gives an otherwise flat-topped block a silhouette.
Institutional and palatial programmes retain the cour d'honneur; the Ecole itself is planned this way.
The free-standing hotel particulier and the exported American mansion reduce to a double-pile block about a central hall and stair.
Irregularity is the antithesis of the parti. Any Beaux-Arts building that appears irregular is resolving a difficult site with a symmetrical figure hidden inside it.

constraints.statement: Every elevation must resolve into base, shaft and attic with distinct horizontal terminations. An undifferentiated wall of repeated identical storeys is not Beaux-Arts, whatever ornament is applied to it.

Sculpture and enrichment must be concentrated at compositional accents - entrance, centrepiece, corners, skyline - and the connecting bays must be comparatively plain. Even distribution of ornament destroys the hierarchy that carries the composition.

Wall thickness must be sufficient to accommodate poche: minimum 600 mm at the principal storeys where stairs, flues or closets are absorbed, and reveals of at least 200 mm at every window so that openings read as cut into mass.

test.note: Tests the minimum wall thickness for poche. The window reveal minimum (200 mm, expressible via reveal_depth_in) is a second independent numeric clause and is left as prose.

constraints.statement: Ornament scale must be calibrated to viewing distance: members read from across a boulevard (25-40 m) should be at least 1/40 of the facade height in their principal dimension. Domestic-scale enrichment on a civic facade reads as thin.

Caractere: the order and level of enrichment must match the programme. Corinthian and Composite with full sculpture for theatres, exhibition and ceremonial buildings; Doric or Tuscan with restrained enrichment for markets, barracks, warehouses and utilitarian programmes.

exemplars.name: Palais Garnier (Opera de Paris)
exemplars.note: Charles Garnier, competition won 1861, built 1861-1875, inaugurated 5 January 1875. The canonical demonstration of marche: the grand escalier and its foyers occupy more of the building than the auditorium.
exemplars.why: The canonical demonstration of marche on this corpus's own reading, and the Mérimée notice supports only who ordered the building, who won the competition - in 1860, not the corpus's 1861 - and that it opened in 1875.

exemplars.name: Grand Palais
exemplars.note: Henri Deglane, Albert Louvet, Albert Thomas and Charles Girault, 1897-1900, for the Exposition Universelle. A Classical stone envelope wrapped around a 240 m iron, steel and glass barrel vault.
exemplars.why: The clearest statement of the Beaux-Arts settlement with iron, and here the register agrees in its own words: 'Parements des façades en pierre de taille ; charpente de la nef en métal et en verre ; béton armé'.

exemplars.name: Petit Palais
exemplars.note: Charles Girault, 1897-1900. A trapezoidal site resolved into a symmetrical parti about a semicircular garden court - the method solving a hard site in the open.
exemplars.why: The corpus's own type specimen for the method solving a hard site, and the register supports none of it - it states no plan, no dimension and no material, and grades the building only 'inscrit' where its twin across the avenue is 'classé'.

exemplars.name: Gare d'Orsay (now Musee d'Orsay)
exemplars.note: Victor Laloux, 1898-1900. An academic stone hotel-and-station front concealing a 32 m clear-span iron train shed; the clearest single statement of the Beaux-Arts settlement with industrial structure.
exemplars.why: A type specimen whose figures the register actually states - a hall 32 m high, 40 m wide and 138 m long behind a stone façade - which is also how this record found that the node has put the 32 m on the wrong axis.

exemplars.name: Bibliotheque Sainte-Genevieve
exemplars.note: Henri Labrouste, campaign years 1844 and 1851 in the Merimee notice. The iron-vaulted reading room over a masonry shell that the node's own prose names as the counter-case to Garnier. THE REGISTER RECORDS NO IRON: it states the architect, the two years, one decor technique and the 1992 classement, and no material and no structure.
exemplars.why: The node's own prose already cites this building as the proof that the method is independent of the dress, and it carried no exemplar for it until this tranche; the standing is the corpus's, because the register supports nothing beyond the architect and the dates.

exemplars.name: La Sorbonne (Nenot rebuilding)
exemplars.note: Henri-Paul Nenot's rebuilding of the university round Lemercier's seventeenth-century chapel; Merimee campaign years 1821, 1824, 1881 and 1901. The 1975 arrete classes five ceremonial circulation spaces individually - grand vestibule, escalier d'honneur, grand amphitheatre, salle des Autorites, grand salon du rectorat - while merely inscribing the whole envelope.
exemplars.why: The academic type, added by this tranche because the node otherwise carried only a theatre, two exhibition halls and a station; and the register's own protection structure is the evidence, protecting the sequence a visitor moves through above the building that contains it.

sources: Julien Guadet, Elements et theorie de l'architecture (1901-1904)
Arthur Drexler (ed.), The Architecture of the Ecole des Beaux-Arts (1977)
David Van Zanten, Designing Paris: The Architecture of Duban, Labrouste, Duc, and Vaudoyer (1987)
Robin Middleton and David Watkin, Neoclassical and 19th Century Architecture (1980)
Jean-Nicolas-Louis Durand, Precis des lecons d'architecture (1802-1805)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The style's caractere doctrine (c05) names Composite directly for 'theatres, exhibition and ceremonial buildings' with full sculpture -- the giant-order register for the Palais Garnier, Grand Palais and Petit Palais register of this style.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. c05 names Corinthian alongside Composite for the same high-caractere programmes; the more restrained of the two richest orders, and the one this style shares directly with beaux-arts-american's own binding.

Bound for the mansard storey rather than for the travee. This node gives 'attic or mansard storey 0.5 to 0.7 of the principal storey height', which is the pack's height_proportion/attic_ratio rule and the reason that rule exists; `storey-graduation` already writes height_proportion/ratio for diminution generally, so the two dimensions are named apart deliberately and both apply. Sits ahead of `facade-classical` by one place only: a Beaux-Arts front is genuinely layered as well as stripped, and this is the one node in the eight where the two systems are close to equals.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs bay division and solid-to-void, though this style pushes every one of the pack's own defaults to its permissive edge: c01's hard requirement that base, shaft and attic resolve with distinct terminations goes well beyond what facade-classical assumes for a domestic front, and the order packs and this style's own constraints carry what the system pack understates.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the void before the surround; a Beaux-Arts opening is often a full aedicule or arched Roman opening rather than the pack's default plain rectangle, so treat its derived ratios as the starting rectangle the surround is built onto.
Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the individual room within the Ecole's axial hierarchy of parti and marche, which is itself outside anything a room-proportion pack models.

Judgment binding: beaux-arts-french is not in storey-graduation's own applies_to (beaux-arts-american is, and carries the identical binding). Bound because this style's own proportional_system states the vertical division directly -- base:shaft:attic approximately 1:2:0.5 -- which is the same diminishing-upward logic the pack encodes, only steeper than its domestic default.

Judgment binding: beaux-arts-french is not in trim-classical's own applies_to (beaux-arts-american is). Bound for the same reason the American branch is: the pedestal:field:entablature wall division is the correct proportional grammar even though real Beaux-Arts interiors ran marble, bronze and run-in-place plaster rather than the pack's default painted joinery -- bind the discipline and expect it executed richer than the pack assumes.
